sections.body_en:
Many mitzvot deal with the subject of the family and with the prohibitions of forbidden relations. The Rambam mentions thirty-six Torah mitzvot in Hilkhot Issurei Bi'a, and together with the mitzvot dealing with the punishments for those who transgress forbidden relations deliberately, after warning and before witnesses, these come to some fifty mitzvot. Even the civilised among the nations of the world have accepted upon themselves the general Torah principles of the prohibitions of forbidden relations, as they are commanded under the seven Noahide mitzvot.

Four kinds of arayot are forbidden. The first part includes every person's own family relatives, such as his mother, his sister, his daughter, his aunt, his brother's wife and his father's wife. When a person marries, a second kind of arayot is added for him, which includes his wife's female relatives, such as her mother, her sister and her daughter. Of course this prohibition applies in parallel to the woman when she marries, regarding her husband's relatives. The third kind admittedly includes only one definition, but in practice most women are included in this definition, and that is the prohibition of a married woman. This prohibition applies from the moment the woman marries her husband, with respect to all the other men in the world. The fourth kind includes two prohibitions that are in the category of changing the order of the world: one is the prohibition of male intercourse (explained in Peninei Halakha, 'Simḥat Ha-Bayit U-Virkhato' 4:13-17), and the second is relations between a person and another species, such as a domestic animal, a wild animal or a bird.

A child born of a forbidden relation has the status of a 'mamzer' (explained below in halakhot 8-10).

A less severe level is having marital relations with a woman who is a nidda, that is, at the time of her period, as long as she has not been purified by immersion in a mikve. However, since in these relations there is no betrayal of a married woman nor a forbidden relation within the family, the severity of this prohibition is less than that of the other prohibitions of adultery, and if a child is born of them, he is not a mamzer.

A lesser level is the prohibition of having marital relations with a woman who is not married, whether single, widowed or divorced, for only within the framework of marriage is it permitted to have marital relations. If she is also a nidda, then a further, more severe prohibition is added to this. In any case, since in these relations there is no betrayal of a married woman nor a forbidden relation within the family, if a child is born of these relations, there is no blemish in him.

There is a further prohibition for a man, to emit seed in vain, since thereby he wastes this power, which was meant to increase joy and love between him and his wife, on a passing desire. And the poskim disagree whether this prohibition is from the Torah or from the words of the Sages (Peninei Halakha, Simḥat Ha-Bayit U-Virkhato 4:1, note 1).

sections.title_en: 2. A Reason for the Prohibition of Arayot
sections.body_en:
The subject of love, its clarification and its direction, is one of the subjects that occupies a person most. Therefore, together with the mitzva to marry in joy and love, the Torah forbade a whole series of arayot: the man's female relatives, his wife's female relatives, a married woman, male intercourse and intercourse with an animal.

Some ask: why does the Torah interfere in a person's feelings and forbid him to show sexual love towards certain people? Many explanations have been given for the prohibitions of arayot, and the wisdom of Kabbala too deals at length with this subject, which is considered one of the three main parts of the hidden wisdom. We will mention here the simple reason.

It is important and even necessary that every person have a supportive and loving environment, a number of people with whom his connection is permanent and not subject to changes. The closest and most supportive environment is the close family – parents, siblings and uncles and aunts – with whom a person shares joyful occasions, and with whom he also manages to overcome troubles and difficulties. If the sexual factor were to enter the picture, with all the tension and competition, the ups and downs involved in it, a person could lose his closest and most supportive environment, and the people who should be most faithful to one another would turn into permanent competitors.

What would happen, Heaven forbid, if a son began to fight with his father over his mother, or if a daughter began to fight with her mother over her father? Or let us try to imagine how, Heaven forbid, family ties could be maintained if a man had to fear at all times that his wife might be tempted by one of her brothers or of his. And likewise, how could a woman live if she always had to fear that her husband might suddenly fall in love with her sister or her mother, or even with her daughter from her previous marriage? If it were permitted for a person to marry his relatives, it is almost certain that sexual tension would break and dismantle the wholeness of the extended family, and the ties between siblings, parents, uncles and aunts would be ties of competition, constant tension and lack of faithfulness.

By virtue of the prohibitions of arayot, the sexual subject has been removed from the family, and for every decent and normal person it does not come up for consideration at all. By virtue of this the family is able to fulfil its role in giving emotional and practical support to each of its sons and daughters. Whereas in a family where these mitzvot are not kept, the simplest feelings develop in a twisted way, and all their lives they try to free themselves from the grievous injury that the forbidden relations inflicted on their souls. This is the simple explanation of the prohibitions of arayot.

In general one can say that all the prohibitions of arayot in the Torah are meant to help a person direct the enormous powers of love into a positive, creative channel, so that the love between the couple will grow and strengthen, for the happiness of the couple and the coming generations.

Of all the prohibitions of arayot, the prohibition that one must most stand guard over and keep is the prohibition of a married woman. For by virtue of the prohibition of forbidden relations within the family, this subject has been removed from the agenda for most people. And from then on a person seeks his partner outside his close family, since he may marry any unmarried woman. But from the moment the woman is betrothed to her husband, she immediately becomes forbidden to the whole world, and what could have been permitted yesterday becomes forbidden today. This is the prohibition of a married woman. And so severe is this prohibition that the Torah established that the punishment for those who transgress it, both for the married woman herself and for the man who committed adultery with her, is death by strangulation. However, in practice there is almost no chance that a person will be punished by strangulation for this act (as explained in the next halakha).

Not only this, but the Torah added a further prohibition, and established that a married woman who committed adultery may no longer continue to live with her husband, and she must divorce him while forgoing the ketuba. And even after her divorce the Torah added a further mitzva forbidding the man and woman who sinned to marry. In other words: a married woman who sinned in adultery has become forbidden to two men for ever: one is her husband, and the second is the one with whom she sinned. (In practice, even if there is a great likelihood that the woman committed adultery, as long as the matter has not been proven completely by witnesses, the beit din sometimes permits the couple to continue living together, and each case is judged in the beit din on its own merits.)

And the most terrible of all is that if a child is born of the married woman's act of adultery, that child is defined as a 'mamzer'. Even a woman who is in the process of divorce, as long as she has not received her get, is a married woman, and if she bears a child to a stranger he will be a mamzer. Further on (in halakhot 10-11) we will explain the laws of the mamzer.

In the previous halakhot we learned that the prohibitions of arayot are considered prohibitions of the most severe level, for most of which the Torah decreed a punishment of death. In this halakha we will briefly survey the system of punishment in the Torah, with an emphasis on the severe punishments of death.

There are several kinds of punishment. Sometimes the Torah sets monetary fines, and sometimes a punishment of thirty-nine lashes, and the most severe punishment is death at the hands of the beit din. Whenever we wish to compare two prohibitions with each other and to know which of them is considered more severe, we check this according to the punishment the Torah set for each prohibition, with the death penalty being the most severe.

Even the death penalty is not uniform. There are four kinds of death by the beit din: strangulation, the sword, burning and stoning. And this is also their order of severity. That is, among the most severe sins, those punished by strangulation are considered lighter, for more severe sins the punishment is the sword, for those more severe still – burning, and for the most severe sins the punishment is stoning. And if, for example, a person committed two transgressions, for one of which he was liable to strangulation and for the second to stoning, he is punished with the more severe death, which is stoning.

The authority to sentence a person to death is given to a Sanhedrin numbering twenty-three expert judges, who were ordained one from another back to Moshe at Sinai. And even the Sanhedrin only very rarely would sentence a person to death, because the beit din is commanded to search as far as possible for merit for those facing death. The Sages already said (Makkot 1:10) that a Sanhedrin that in the course of seven years decreed death for one person was considered a destructive Sanhedrin, because it frequently kills those judged before it. And in the view of Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, even if it decreed death only once in seventy years, it would be considered a destructive Sanhedrin. And Rabbi Akiva said that had he been a member of the Sanhedrin, they would never have sentenced a person to death in it, for he would always find a side of merit according to which the sinner is exempt from the death penalty. And against him Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel said: "They too would multiply shedders of blood in Israel"; and from this we learn that those executed by the beit din were mainly murderers.

The reason for this is clear: the halakha is that a person is not executed unless there were two witnesses who warned him and nevertheless he continued in his sin. That is, if it concerns a sin of forbidden relations, there must be two people who warn the sinners that if they continue in their adultery they will be punished with death. And this is not a matter of witnesses who saw them entering a closed room, but of witnesses who see them actually committing the sin. And before that they warned them and said: know that if you sin you will be punished with death; and the sinners know that the beit din has the authority and the power to carry out the sentence on them, and nevertheless they continue to commit their sin. There is no person who would sin under such conditions. Therefore there were almost no situations in which the beit din executed a person for sins of forbidden relations or desecration of Shabbat. And from this it follows that the death penalties the Torah set for the sins of forbidden relations and the other transgressions were meant to define the severity of the transgression and to prevent it being committed in front of people. The only severe transgression that was sometimes committed in front of witnesses is murder, for murder is committed in a moment of anger, and witnesses and warning do not always help. Therefore Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel said that if the beit din increases side examinations of the witnesses in order to disqualify them, it will cause an increase in bloodshed. And even the execution of murderers was not meant for frequent use. And so we have learned (Avoda Zara 8b) that when murderers increased, the Great Sanhedrin went into exile from the Chamber of Hewn Stone to a place called Ḥanut, and thereby the authority was lost from the lesser Sanhedrin, which was in every city throughout the land, to sentence murderers to death.1

notes_en.en: The only case in which sinners might continue in their sin despite the witnesses and the warning is murder, for murder is committed in a moment of anger. Indeed the people who were executed in the beit din were deliberate murderers, as emerges from Mishna Makkot 1:10: "A Sanhedrin that executes one in a week (in seven years) is called destructive. Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya says: one in seventy years. Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva say: had we been in the Sanhedrin, no person would ever have been executed. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says: they too would multiply shedders of blood in Israel." So the main application of the death penalty was to murderers; and so we have learned in the Gemara, Avoda Zara 8b, that when murderers increased, the Sanhedrin went into exile from the Chamber of Hewn Stone to Ḥanut, in order to give up the authority to sentence murderers to death. For execution was meant for deterrence and not for frequent use.

sections.body_en:
Most of the prohibitions of arayot are connected to family relatives. In general, one can divide the kinds of relatives into two main parts. One is the relatives of every person by virtue of his being born into his family, such as the son with his mother or the father with his daughter, and likewise a brother with his sister, or a son with his aunt. And the second kind of prohibitions of arayot begins from the moment the person marries.

Every person who marries immediately becomes forbidden to seven women related to his wife. Six of them are forbidden to him for ever; that is, even if he divorces his wife or is widowed, he will be forbidden to marry them. And one is forbidden to him as long as his wife is alive.

These are the six women forbidden to him for ever: his wife's mother, her grandmother on her mother's side, and her grandmother on her father's side, and her daughter if she had one from a previous marriage, and likewise her granddaughter through her son or her granddaughter through her daughter. In other words, three relatives upwards and three downwards. The three upwards are: his wife's mother, her grandmother on her mother's side and her grandmother on her father's side. And if the woman already had children from a previous marriage, then three kinds of women downwards are also forbidden to him, and these are: his wife's daughter, and likewise her granddaughter through her daughter and likewise her granddaughter through her son. As we have learned, all these women are forbidden to him for ever, and even after his wife's death he will be forbidden to marry them.

But his wife's sister is the seventh woman who becomes forbidden to him from the moment he married, and she is forbidden to him only while his wife is alive; and if he is widowed, he may marry her.

A man may not marry his aunt, but he may marry his niece. The difference depends on the question of who is the groom and who is the bride. If the bride is the aunt, the marriage is forbidden; and if they married and a child was born to them, he is a mamzer. But if the groom is the uncle, and the bride is the daughter of his sister or the daughter of his brother, they may marry.

Let us explain in more detail the prohibition of marrying an aunt. There are four kinds of aunts. Two kinds are his parents' sisters – the father's sister or the mother's sister. And there are two more kinds of aunts by marriage, who are: the woman who married his father's brother and the woman who married his mother's brother; and these too are forbidden to him for ever, so that even if they were widowed or divorced, since through their marriage they became his aunts, they are forbidden to him for ever.

And although in practice all four of these aunts are forbidden, there is a distinction between them: three of them are forbidden by the Torah and one by the words of the Sages. The father's sister, the mother's sister and also the woman who married the father's brother are forbidden by the Torah. But one who was his aunt by marriage to the mother's brother is forbidden by the words of the Sages, and in this case, if they sinned and a child was born of their sin, he is not a mamzer, for a mamzer is one born of Torah prohibitions whose punishment is severe. This rabbinic prohibition is called 'sheniyot la-arayot' (secondary forbidden relations); further examples of these rabbinic prohibitions: grandmothers of their various kinds, and the wives of grandsons and great-grandsons.2

notes_en.en:
Most of the 'sheniyot la-arayot' are rare situations. We will mention the list of all the secondary relations that the Sages forbade, as the Rambam summarised them, Hilkhot Ishut 1:6: "There are other women who are forbidden by tradition, and their prohibition is from the words of the scribes, and they are called sheniyot, because they are secondary to the arayot, and each of them is called a sheniya; and they are twenty women, and these are they: 1) his mother's mother, and this has no end, but even his mother's mother's mother's mother, upwards without limit, is forbidden; 2) his mother's father's mother only; 3) and his father's mother, and this has no end, but even his father's mother's mother's mother upwards is forbidden; 4) his father's father's mother only; 5) his father's father's wife, and this has no end, even the wife of Yaakov our father is forbidden to each one of us; 6) his mother's father's wife only; 7) the wife of his father's maternal brother; 8) the wife of his mother's brother, whether maternal or paternal; 9) his son's daughter-in-law, and this has no end, even the daughter-in-law of his son's son's son to the end of the world is forbidden, so that the wife of one of us would be a sheniya to Yaakov our father; 10) his daughter's daughter-in-law only; 11) his son's daughter's daughter only; 12) his son's son's daughter only; 13) his daughter's daughter's daughter only; 14) his daughter's son's daughter only; 15) the daughter of his wife's son's son only; 16) the daughter of his wife's daughter's daughter only; 17) the mother of his wife's father's mother only; 18) the mother of his wife's mother's father only; 19) the mother of his wife's mother's mother only;
20) the mother of his wife's father's father only. So the secondary relations that have no end are four: the mother's mother upwards, the father's mother upwards, the father's father's wife upwards, and the wife of his son's son downwards."

sections.body_en:
One of the prohibitions of arayot is the prohibition of a brother with his sister. And this prohibition exists also when the sister is only on his mother's side, or only on his father's side. Not only this, but even if they were born to the same father outside marriage – for example, their father never married at all, and was promiscuous with several women, and from one he fathered a son and from the second a daughter – even then they are considered siblings and may not marry. And likewise the law in the reverse case, when their mother bore them outside marriage from two different men: these too are considered siblings and are forbidden. As it is said (Vayikra 18:9): "The nakedness of your sister, the daughter of your father or the daughter of your mother, whether born at home or born outside, you shall not uncover their nakedness."

To prevent such a case, in which a brother and sister born outside marriage would marry each other, the Rabbinate keeps a list of those unfit to marry, in which there also appear lists of brothers and sisters who were born outside marriage and afterwards given up for adoption. And it has already happened that a couple came to the Rabbinate to receive approval for marriage, and when they opened the lists it turned out that the applicants were siblings. With great delicacy they revealed the matter to them, and they refrained from marrying. Likewise a son and a daughter born from the same sperm donor are considered siblings and may not marry.

But in a case where a widow who has a son married a widower who has a daughter, and likewise the reverse, their children are not considered siblings, and they may marry each other.

sections.title_en: 8. Conception from Seed That Is Not the Husband's
sections.body_en:
There was a case of a woman who married, and more than ten years passed and she had still not given birth, and the doctors said that the reason for this depended on the husband, that there was a defect in his seed and he could not father children. The doctors took the seed of another man and placed it in her womb, and from this a child was born to her. And the question was asked: is the son who was born considered a fit Jew, or perhaps he is a mamzer, unfit to enter the congregation and to marry a Jewish woman?

The basis of the question is the halakha that a married woman who committed adultery with another man, and a son was born to her from him, is a mamzer, and he may not marry a woman of the seed of Israel, as explained in the next halakha. The question then is: what is the law when a woman bore a child from seed that is not her husband's, but without an act of forbidden relations having been done?

According to halakha, the children born in this way are not mamzerim, because the definition of a mamzer is one whose birth was caused by a severe act of forbidden relations, such that had the transgression been done deliberately, with warning and before witnesses, they would have been liable to death for it – as, for example, a son born of a father who was promiscuous with his daughter, or a man who committed adultery with a married woman. But in a case where the conception was done without an act of promiscuity, the child born is fit to enter the congregation. Not only this, but if a daughter is born of this, she may marry a kohen; that is, there is no defect at all in children born in this way (Igrot Moshe EH 1:10).

As to the act itself, the poskim disagree on the question whether it is permitted ideally for a woman whose husband is infertile to conceive from seed taken from another man. Some are stringent and some are lenient, and in any such painful case one should ask a Torah scholar.

The most severe practical consequence that may be caused by an act of promiscuity is the birth of a son or daughter whose halakhic definition is 'mamzer'. And about this the Sages said: "What is a crooked thing that cannot be made straight? This is one who has relations with an erva and fathers a mamzer son" (Ḥagiga 9b). For in addition to those people having committed a severe sin whose punishment according to the Torah is strangulation, and without witnesses and warning its punishment is karet, that is, death at the hands of Heaven, even the children who will be born to them from this will be forbidden to marry anyone of the congregation of Israel. Admittedly a male or female convert may marry a mamzer, but the children who will be born to them will also be in the same trouble, and will not be able to marry anyone of the seed of Israel. In other words, as long as one of the parents is a mamzer, the children who will be born will also be mamzerim. Therefore it is reasonable that a male or female convert would not agree to marry a mamzer, so as not to disqualify their descendants.

This is the rule: a mamzer child is one born of an act of forbidden relations involving a Torah prohibition whose punishment from the Torah is death or karet – for example, one born of the promiscuity of a brother with his sister, or of the adultery of a married woman with a stranger. And as long as the woman has not yet received a get and her husband is alive, even though she is already in the process of divorce, she is still considered a married woman, and if a child is born to her from a stranger, that child will be a mamzer.

But a man who had relations with an unmarried woman without marriage, although there is a prohibition of promiscuity in this, there is no prohibition of karet here, and the child is not a mamzer. And even if the woman was impure as a nidda (who had not immersed after her period), the child born to her is not a mamzer. And although the prohibition of nidda is severe and its punishment is karet, the Sages said that this is the only case in which a child born of a prohibition whose punishment is karet is not considered a mamzer. Admittedly there is a blemish in his lineage, but this blemish does not disqualify him from marrying even with families of priestly lineage (SA EH 4:13; Be'er Heitev 11).

We do not presume to know the absolute reason for the mitzvot of the Torah, for the Creator's thoughts are higher than our thoughts. But one can understand that through this terrible decree of mamzerut, the Torah fights with all its force against the problem of promiscuity. For there is nothing more terrible and destructive for the wholeness of the family and the education of the children than promiscuity. Of course, in order to strengthen family love one must mainly encourage the good qualities of love, patience and respect. But in addition to the good inclination a person also has an evil inclination, and sometimes he tends to be tempted by a momentary desire that in the end could destroy his family. And then only a most severe punishment, which expresses the severity of the flawed act itself, can deter him from the act of betrayal.

Indeed this harsh punishment is extremely deterrent, and admittedly on rare occasions there are people who suffer greatly from it; but on the other hand, the general benefit that flows from it to the whole of society cannot be measured. Of course this is only one simple reason, and everyone who believes in the Torah understands that there are also deeper reasons, and the Creator of the world and of souls knows the secret of the order of the unfolding of souls.

It is further important to add that the terrible blemish in a mamzer is specifically with regard to marriage; but with regard to all the rest of the Torah the mamzer is equal to every Jew. And he can even rise in the levels of holiness and reach a high level. And so the Sages said in the Mishna (Horayot 3:8) that one should give precedence and honour to a mamzer who is a Torah scholar over a High Priest who is ignorant.

There is only one way for a male mamzer to father children who will in the end be able to marry any Jewish man or woman, and whose descendants will be fit. To explain the matter, let us repeat what we have learned. The hard problem facing the mamzer is that he has almost no possibility of marrying, since according to the Torah he may not marry a Jewish woman. Only if he finds a woman who is a mamzeret, who was also born of a prohibition, will they be permitted to marry. But this will not help their children, for they will pass on mamzerut to their sons and daughters. And likewise a mamzer may marry a female convert, but since mamzerut will pass to their children, it is reasonable that no convert will be found who will agree to marry a mamzer.

Only one way stands open to the mamzer through which he can make his descendants fit, and that is through a maidservant. And what is meant here is a gentile woman who comes to be a maidservant to a Jew; according to Torah law, when she accepts upon herself to be a maidservant to a Jew, she must undergo a process of partial conversion that includes immersion and accepting mitzvot, and from then on she must keep the mitzvot. And if she is freed, she will not be able to return to her former people, and on the spot she is considered Jewish. If so, on the one hand she has the law of a gentile, and any Jew who fathers a child from a gentile woman – the child does not inherit his lineage from him, and he is considered like his gentile mother in every respect, for nationality is determined by the mother. If so, also in this case of the mamzer and the maidservant, the child does not inherit mamzerut from him, since he is not reckoned after his father, and he is considered a slave like his mother. And on the other hand, if the maidservant were an ordinary gentile, the mamzer would be forbidden to marry her, and the children born to her would also be complete gentiles. But here, since the maidservant has already begun a process of conversion, they permitted the mamzer to marry her, and the children who will be born to them are considered slaves who are obligated in most of the mitzvot; and immediately after they are born they can be freed, and through this they will be considered fit Jews, like any Canaanite slave who went free.

And although by law a Jew may not marry a maidservant, for a mamzer they permitted this in order to make his descendants fit (SA EH 4:20). And the Radbaz wrote that there was a case in Constantinople of a mamzer who was a Torah scholar who married a maidservant, and the sages of Constantinople gathered at his wedding in his honour.

And although according to halakha, in our socio-economic situation slavery is forbidden – for slavery was permitted only when without it many of those people would have been likely to die of hunger, but today, when it is possible to provide for them, slavery is forbidden (see Peninei Halakha, Shevi'it Ve-Yovel 10:11) – nevertheless, in order to make the descendants of the mamzer fit, it will be permitted to apply the law of the maidservant, although in practice she must be treated like an ordinary wife; and to a certain extent it is even fitting that he honour her more, since she agreed to be his maidservant in order to help him make his descendants fit.

sections.title_en: 11. A Convert Is Forbidden to His Relatives Rabbinically
sections.body_en:
According to Torah law, a convert who has converted is like a newborn child, and all the family ties he had with his parents and siblings are cancelled, and he is no longer considered related to them.

It follows from this that if, for example, a mother and her son convert, since they converted they are no longer considered relatives, and they would be permitted to marry each other. And likewise a brother and sister who converted would, by Torah law, be permitted to marry.

But by the words of the Sages the matter is forbidden, so that the converts should not say: we have come from a more severe holiness to a lighter holiness. For the gentiles too are commanded to keep some of the laws of arayot, under the seven Noahide mitzvot. If so, when they were gentiles a son was forbidden to marry his mother; how could it be that after he converts it would be permitted? Therefore the Sages established that even after the conversion, all the prohibitions of arayot that applied to the convert when he was a gentile remain upon him.

Incidentally, it is worth mentioning here the six prohibitions of arayot that are imposed not only on Israel but also on all the children of Noaḥ, and these are: a mother, a father's wife, a sister on the mother's side, a married woman, male intercourse, and intercourse with an animal.

Male kohanim may not marry certain women, since they have been consecrated to the service of the Temple, as it is said (Vayikra 21:1-7): "And the Lord said to Moshe: Speak to the kohanim, the sons of Aharon… They shall be holy to their God and shall not profane the name of their God, for the fire offerings of the Lord, the bread of their God, they offer, and they shall be holy. A woman who is a harlot or profaned they shall not take, and a woman divorced from her husband they shall not take, for he is holy to his God." For the daughters of a kohen there are no restrictions; rather whoever is fit to marry a daughter of Israel is fit to marry a daughter of a kohen.

These are the women forbidden to a kohen: a zona, a ḥalala, a divorcee, a ḥalutza and a convert. A zona is one who had relations with a man whom she is forbidden to marry, such as a gentile, or in a forbidden relation within the family; and even if she was raped by him, she has become forbidden to a kohen. But one who had relations with a Jew whom by law she is permitted to marry is not considered a zona. A ḥalutza is one who was married and her husband died without having had a child from her, so that there is a Torah mitzva that his brother perform yibbum with her, that is, marry her in order to father a son who will continue the first husband who died. And if the brother is not willing to do this, then the widow of the deceased brother removes his shoe and a certain formula is said, and with this she is released from him; but her law is like that of a divorcee, who is forbidden to a kohen. A ḥalala is the daughter of a ḥalal, that is, the daughter of a kohen whose holiness was profaned because he was born to a kohen who married a woman forbidden to him, such as a divorcee. And so the law continues to the end of all generations, that every daughter born to the descendants of ḥalalim is forbidden to a kohen.
